01.note: Rabbi Yannai owned a tree that leaned out over the public road, and so did another man. The public objected to the other man's tree, and he came to Rabbi Yannai for a ruling. Rabbi Yannai told him to go and come back tomorrow, and that night he had his own tree cut down. When the man returned, Rabbi Yannai told him to cut his tree. The man protested that the master had one too, and Rabbi Yannai answered: go and look; if mine is cut down, cut yours, and if not, you need not cut yours either.
01.why: The mishna forbids things that jut out into the public domain, and Rabbi Ami has just ordered a man to cut a projection. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Yannai's delay with Reish Lakish's teaching: set yourself right first, and only then correct others.

02.note: After the Second Temple was destroyed, many Jews became ascetics who refused to eat meat or drink wine, because meat had been offered on the altar and wine poured on it, and the altar was gone. Rabbi Yehoshua joined them and argued: then we should not eat bread, since the meal-offerings have ceased; they answered they could live on produce. Then not fruit, since the first fruits have ceased; they said other produce would do. Then not water, since the water libation has ceased. They fell silent. He told them that not mourning at all is impossible, but mourning too much is also impossible, since the Sages impose no decree that most of the public cannot keep.
02.why: The Gemara has been discussing a ruling that people may not plaster their houses as a sign of mourning for the Temple. Rabbi Yehoshua's answer to the ascetics leads into the measured rule that follows: plaster the house, but leave a small patch bare in remembrance.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who reasons with the ascetics and teaches them how to mourn.

terms.meaning: People who deny themselves ordinary pleasures; here, Jews who gave up meat and wine in mourning.

03.note: Rabba reports what seafarers told him: when a wave that is about to sink a ship comes with a ray of white fire at its head, they strike it with clubs inscribed with names of God, and the wave calms down.
03.why: The Gemara has been discussing what is included when a ship is sold, and from there turns to a series of tales about ships and the sea.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who passes on what sailors told him.

04.note: Rabba passes on a seafarers' tale. Waves can be three hundred parasangs apart and three hundred parasangs high. Once a wave lifted their ship so high that they saw the resting place of a small star, as large as a field sown with forty se'a of mustard seed, and had it lifted them higher they would have been scorched. Then one wave called to another: did you leave anything in the world unwashed, that I may destroy it? The other answered: see the power of your Master; I cannot pass even a strip of sand, and it quoted Jeremiah's verse about God setting sand as the bound of the sea.
04.why: It follows the Gemara's discussion of what comes with a ship that is sold, as part of a run of tales about ships and the sea.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who passes on what sailors told him.

terms.meaning: An ancient Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
A measure of volume for grain or seed; forty se'a of mustard seed would sow a large field.

05.note: Rabba says he saw Hurmin, son of Lilith, running along the tops of the walls of Mehoza so fast that a horseman riding below could not catch him. Once two mules were saddled for him, standing on two bridges of the river Rognag, and he leapt from one to the other and back, pouring wine between two cups in his hands without spilling a drop, on a stormy day. Word of this reached the king's house, and they killed him.
05.why: It is one of a series of marvels the Gemara collects after the seafarers' tales.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who says he saw these things himself.

people.name: Hurmin, son of Lilith
people.about: A demon-like figure who performs impossible feats until the king's men kill him.

terms.meaning: In Jewish lore, a female demon; calling Hurmin her son marks him as a supernatural being.

06.note: Rabba says he saw a day-old antelope as big as Mount Tabor, which is four parasangs. Its neck was three parasangs long and the place where its head rested was a parasang and a half. Its dung dammed up the Jordan River.
06.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba

07.note: Rabba bar bar Hana says he saw a frog as big as the fort of Hagronya, which is the size of sixty houses. A snake came and swallowed the frog, then a raven came and swallowed the snake and flew up to sit in a tree. Think how strong that tree must have been. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel said that had he not been there, he would not have believed it.
07.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

08.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a huge fish that had been killed by a tiny mud-eating creature lodged in its nostril. The sea threw it on the shore, and it destroyed sixty districts; sixty districts ate from it and sixty salted its meat, and three hundred flasks of oil were filled from one eyeball. When they came back a year later, people were sawing beams from its bones to rebuild the districts it had destroyed.
08.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

09.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a fish so old that sand had settled on its back and grass grew there. Thinking it was dry land, they climbed onto it and baked and cooked. When its back grew hot, the fish turned over, and had the ship not been close by they would have drowned.
09.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

10.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which the ship sailed for three days and three nights between one fin of a fish and the other, the fish swimming upstream and the ship downstream. Lest anyone think the ship was slow, Rav Dimi said such a ship covers sixty parasangs in the time it takes to heat a kettle of water, and outran an arrow shot by a horseman. Rav Ashi said the fish was a sea gildana, which has two sets of fins.
10.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

11.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a bird standing in water up to its ankles, with its head in the sky. Thinking the water was shallow, they wanted to go down to cool off, but a Divine Voice told them not to: a carpenter's ax had fallen in there seven years earlier and still had not reached the bottom, because the water is so turbulent. Rav Ashi said the bird was the ziz sadai named in Psalms.
11.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

12.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of crossing the desert and seeing geese so fat their wings drooped, with streams of oil flowing beneath them. He asked them: will we have a share of you in the World-to-Come? One raised a wing and one raised a leg. When he told Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Elazar said the Jewish people will be held to account for those geese.
12.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

13.note: Crossing the desert, Rabba bar bar Hana traveled with an Arab who could tell the road, and how far they were from water, by smelling the dust; Rabba bar bar Hana tried to trick him by switching the dust and could not. The Arab showed him the dead of the wilderness, the Israelites who died after leaving Egypt, lying on their backs and looking drunk, so huge that the Arab rode a camel under one man's raised knee with his spear upright. Rabba bar bar Hana cut a corner of one of their fringed garments, and they could not move until he returned it. When he told the Sages, they called him a donkey and an idiot: if he wanted to settle how many threads belong in fringes, he should simply have counted them.
13.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

14.note: The Arab guide also took Rabba bar bar Hana to Mount Sinai, which was ringed by scorpions as tall as white donkeys. There he heard a Divine Voice saying: woe is Me that I took an oath, and now who will release Me from it? When he told the Sages, they called him a donkey and an idiot, saying he should have answered: your oath is released. The Gemara explains that he thought it might be God's oath never to bring another flood, and the Sages reply that then God would not have said woe is Me.
14.why: It is one of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, part of a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

15.note: The Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana the place where Korah's followers were swallowed by the earth: two cracks giving off smoke. The Arab dipped a tuft of wool in water, put it on the tip of his spear and held it in, and it came out scorched. He told Rabba bar bar Hana to listen, and he heard them saying: Moses and his Torah are true, and we are liars. The Arab said that every thirty days Gehenna brings them back to this spot, like meat turning in a pot, and each time they say this.
15.why: It is one of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, part of a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

16.note: The Arab guide offered to show Rabba bar bar Hana the place where earth and sky touch. Rabba bar bar Hana set his basket down in a window of the sky, and when he finished praying it was gone. He asked whether there were thieves here. The Arab said no: the sphere of the heavens was turning, and if he waited until tomorrow he would find it again.
16.why: It is the last of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, in a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

17.note: Rabbi Yohanan tells of a voyage on which they saw a crate set with precious stones and pearls, circled by sharks. A diver went down to bring it up, and the sharks, enraged, tried to tear off his thigh, but he threw a flask of vinegar at them and they sank away. Then a Divine Voice told them: what business do you have with the crate of the wife of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa? She is destined to put sky-blue wool in it for the fringes of the righteous in the World-to-Come.
17.why: It is one of a run of sea tales the Gemara strings together, this one told by Rabbi Yohanan.

18.note: Rav Yehuda from India tells of a voyage on which they saw a precious stone circled by a sea serpent. A diver went down for it, and the serpent tried to swallow the ship. A raven cut off its head and the water turned to blood. Another serpent came, hung the stone on the dead one, and it came back to life and again tried to swallow the ship. A bird cut off its head and threw the stone onto the ship. The travelers had some salted birds with them; they put the stone on them, and the birds took the stone and flew away with it.
18.why: It closes a run of travelers' tales about sea creatures; the Gemara then turns to the great sea creatures mentioned in the Bible.

people.name: Rav Yehuda from India
people.about: The Sage who tells what he saw on a voyage.

19.note: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were traveling by ship. Rabbi Eliezer was asleep and Rabbi Yehoshua awake, and Rabbi Yehoshua trembled, waking Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer asked why he trembled, and Rabbi Yehoshua said he had seen a great light in the sea. Rabbi Eliezer answered that perhaps he had seen the eyes of the leviathan, quoting Job: his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.
19.why: After the travelers' tales of huge sea creatures, the Gemara turns to the sea creatures of the Bible; this account opens its discussion of the leviathan and the great sea monsters of Genesis.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage traveling by ship who suggests what his companion saw.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who sees a great light in the sea and trembles.

terms.meaning: A giant sea creature described in the Bible, especially in the book of Job.

20.note: Rav Ashi reports that Huna bar Natan told him: crossing the desert with a thigh of meat, they cut it open, removed the forbidden sinew and fat, and laid it on the grass. By the time they brought firewood the meat had healed itself whole, and they roasted it. A year later they came back and found the coals still glowing. Ameimar explained that the grass was a herb of life and the coals were from broom wood.
20.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by various Sages, that the Gemara strings together one after another.
